prompt: You run 40 app servers, each with an in-process cache of user profiles (TTL 10 minutes). Assume no stale in-flight refill or replica lag, and no invalidation on writes. A user changes their display name. What will they most likely experience?

options.text: The name flips between old and new on refresh, depending on which server the load balancer picks, for up to 10 minutes
options.explanation: Correct. Each server has its own copy. Servers that cached the old name keep serving it until their entry expires, so requests landing on different servers see different values.

options.text: The new name appears everywhere immediately, because the database was updated
options.explanation: The database is updated, but 40 independent in-process caches still hold the old value until their TTL expires or they are explicitly invalidated.

options.text: The old name appears for exactly 10 minutes on every server, then changes everywhere at once
options.explanation: Each server cached the profile at a different time, so each entry expires at a different moment. There is no single synchronised switch-over.

options.text: The update fails, because in-process caches lock the row
options.explanation: In-process caches hold copies; they do not take database locks. The write succeeds.

workedExample:
1. In-process means **one cache per server**: 40 separate copies.
2. Server A cached the profile at 10:00, server B at 10:07, server C never cached it.
3. The user renames at 10:08.
4. A request to C misses and reads the new name. A request to A shows the old name until 10:10. B shows it until 10:17.
5. The load balancer spreads requests, so the user sees the name flicker.

Fixes: use a shared cache with reliable invalidation (Redis alone does not ensure freshness), shorten the in-process TTL to a few seconds, or broadcast invalidations (for example via Redis pub/sub).

prompt: You are choosing between an in-process cache and a shared Redis cache for product data on 30 app servers. Which statements are true? Select all that apply.

options.text: An in-process lookup avoids a network round trip and can reduce latency.
options.explanation: Correct. The actual cost depends on language, data structure, serialization and workload; there is no universal 100 ns application lookup guarantee.

options.text: With one coalesced cold fill per server, up to 30 independent servers may load the same key.
options.explanation: Correct under that assumption. Without per-process coalescing, concurrent misses can produce more than one load per server.

options.text: A Redis cache is lost whenever an app server is redeployed
options.explanation: Incorrect. Redis runs as a separate service, so it survives app deploys. It is the in-process cache that is emptied on every restart.

options.text: An in-process cache keeps all 30 servers consistent with each other automatically
options.explanation: Incorrect. Each server holds an independent copy, so they can disagree until each entry expires or is invalidated.

options.text: A small in-process cache with a 1–5 s TTL in front of Redis can absorb very hot keys
options.explanation: Correct when short local staleness is acceptable. Local TTL bounds time since insertion, not total age inherited from Redis or a lagging source.

workedExample:
1. Local caches avoid the network but each process has its own contents.
2. Shared Redis centralizes access, but replicas, invalidation races and stale origin data still affect consistency with the database.
3. A separate Redis service survives app restarts; a process-local cache does not.
4. Combining tiers can reduce hot-key load; measure latency and include every layer when setting freshness objectives.
